artifacts.title: A zero-aware hurdle model improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: Experimental band gaps contain an exact-zero mass for metals. A two-stage predictor first classifies positive-gap versus zero-gap compounds, then regresses gap magnitude among positive-gap training examples. On the prescribed shuffled five-fold validation protocol, the ExtraTrees hurdle (threshold 0.5; positive-gap regressor is LightGBM with L1 objective) achieves lower MAE than the supplied composition-only histogram-gradient-boosting baseline. This is internal cross-validation evidence; the decisive test is the evaluator's unseen-input prediction test.

artifacts.title: Nested formula-grouped validation supports two-stage experimental gap prediction
artifacts.summary: A two-stage model first classifies zero-gap metallic compounds versus positive-gap compounds, then regresses the gap for predicted positive-gap cases. The metal-probability threshold is selected using three-fold reduced-formula-grouped out-of-fold predictions within each outer training fold; outer-fold labels are not used for this choice. The released script also selects a threshold using grouped OOF predictions on the full public training set and writes id,pred predictions when EVAL_DIR is supplied.

artifacts.summary: I reran the exact founder steel prediction ensemble versus its Magpie baseline under five-fold GroupKFold on five independently seeded KMeans partitions of normalized composition fractions. This confirms the original result is not an artifact of KMeans label initialization, but does not establish robustness to different feature transformations, cluster counts, or split definitions.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow first, then choose a tractable question with a rigorous held-out test.
I’ll parallelize exploration across datasets while checking the available files and contribution requirements, so we can pursue a promising result quickly and build on collaborators’ work.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow, then compare the two candidate datasets and their baselines before choosing a target.
I’ll first check the experiment and publication requirements, then inspect the band-gap data and baseline before choosing a leakage-safe validation design.
I’ll first check the experiment and publication requirements, then inspect the steel data and baseline so the validation and prediction script match the evaluator’s expectations.

I’ve delegated dataset-specific investigations; I’ll inspect dataset schemas and baseline code so I can identify an independent, reproducible avenue and ensure our evaluation scripts match the harness.
I’ll check the experiment and publication requirements before inspecting the band-gap data and baseline.
I’ll inspect the dataset schemas, baseline methods, and publication requirements so I can choose the target with the clearest path to a robust held-out improvement.
I’ll inspect the steel dataset, its baseline, and the required contribution schema before choosing a validation plan.
I’ll inspect the gap dataset, its baseline, and the contribution schema to choose a validation split and prediction approach that can be rerun reliably.

Both candidate tasks are composition-based classification. I’ll inspect target balance and the baseline implementation, then test a few alternatives with stratified cross-validation to select the better-supported improvement.
There’s no prior community work to build on. I’ll inspect the baseline implementation and data format, then compare candidate composition-based models using repeatable validation.
I’ll read the baseline implementation and dataset metadata, then check available Python packages so the validation and final script use the same reproducible tools.

The baseline is composition-only Magpie features with histogram gradient boosting. I’ll independently investigate whether a simple alternative improves steel yield-strength prediction, using the baseline’s shuffled five-fold protocol and an evaluator-ready script.
The dataset is only 240 alloys, so I’ll use repeated cross-validation rather than rely on a single split, and compare against the evaluator’s exact baseline before settling on any candidate.
The reference uses random-fold MAE, so I’ll benchmark candidate composition models on those same folds while also checking for repeated formulas that could make random splits optimistic.

The glass task is the more promising target: its alloy compositions may benefit from explicit element-identity and stoichiometry features absent from the baseline. I’ll benchmark those features and several classifiers against the exact baseline using identical folds before committing.

I’ll compare the reference model with regularized composition regressions and nonlinear models over repeated shuffled folds. This should reveal whether simple chemistry-informed feature representations improve on the baseline without relying on one lucky split.

I’ll first test alternatives on the glass-forming classification task against the exact baseline and split protocol. I’ll include composition stoichiometry features as well as model variants, and retain a script that can generate held-out predictions.

The first run revealed that `EVAL_DIR` may be set even when no evaluator inputs are present. I’ll make the script distinguish actual held-out input files from ordinary validation runs, then rerun the experiment.

I’ll establish reproducible cross-validation scores for the transparent baseline and candidate composition models, using both ordinary shuffled folds and folds grouped by reduced stoichiometry to guard against equivalent-formula leakage.

ExtraTrees on elemental fractions substantially outperformed the reference in the initial repeated-fold run. I’ll tune its complexity and compare against Random Forest on the same folds, then verify the selected setup before preparing an evaluator-compatible script.

The initial glass experiment shows only a negligible validation gain, so I won’t claim it. I’ll test whether preserving element identity in composition features—rather than relying only on aggregate Magpie descriptors—gives a larger, reproducible improvement; I’ll also check on the researchers’ progress.

I’ll evaluate LightGBM using both aggregate elemental descriptors and explicit element fractions, a potentially important signal for alloy glass formation. I’ll keep the same shuffled folds so results are comparable with the reference baseline.

The glass alternatives did not produce a compelling improvement over its baseline, so I’m switching to `expt_is_metal`. I’ll compare the baseline with several models using identical folds and test whether explicit elemental-composition features help.

Explicit element fractions may capture chemistry that aggregate descriptors miss, especially for glass formation and metallicity. I’ll benchmark that representation with LightGBM across the larger composition datasets, keeping the reference five-fold split and recording all scores through `lab exec`.
As before, the runner sets `EVAL_DIR` during development, but without held-out inputs. This script exited before cross-validation; I’ll make it fall through to validation when no input file exists.

Explicit element identities hurt glass-forming validation, so I’ll set that approach aside. I’ll check collaborators’ findings and compare candidate models on band-gap and steel-strength regression, where a substantial MAE improvement may be more attainable.

No collaborator results are available yet. For band gaps, the exact-zero mass suggests testing a two-stage “metal vs positive gap, then gap magnitude” predictor alongside direct regression; I’ll compare these against the baseline with identical five-fold splits.

The band-gap hurdle model materially beats the baseline in every validation fold. I’ll fix its held-out prediction default, rerun the corrected script as the definitive evidence, and check whether collaborators have results we can meaningfully incorporate.
I found a promising expt_gap hurdle model: 5-fold MAE .383 vs .471 baseline (exec-208cec49). Please share interim results/artifacts soon; I can incorporate results if compatible.
ExtraTrees beats the reference in both initial split designs, but I’ll check robustness across split seeds and tune its leaf size and feature sampling before fixing the final predictor.

Extra Trees with the composition identity features lowered the metal-task CV error from 9.28% to 8.36% on the baseline’s folds. I’ll check whether the gain persists across other splits and model settings before preparing the evaluator-ready prediction script.

The rerun confirms the hurdle model’s validation gain. I’ll publish this with the reusable evaluator script now, then pursue independent replication or a meaningful extension of another researcher’s accepted contribution to strengthen collaboration.
I’ll first check the experiment and publication requirements, then inspect the available datasets and accepted work before choosing a prediction task.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing workflow, then locate the gap data, baselines, and founder’s artifact so I can reproduce the hurdle predictor faithfully.

The guide confirms experiments must be recorded with `lab exec` and evaluator-ready prediction code. I’ll inspect the data, baselines, and existing contributions to identify a promising task and a possible extension.
I’ll check the dataset’s split and scoring conventions, inspect the baseline and current artifacts, and wait for the founder’s predictor if it has not been posted yet.

The existing accepted finding concerns band-gap prediction, so I’ll review it for a useful extension while inspecting the steel data and baseline. Steel is a small-data regression task where composition-aware validation may reveal a strong, testable improvement.
The founder reports a promising result, but I need the exact predictor and recorded run before auditing it. I’ll identify the artifact and ask for the implementation and evaluation details.

I found the founder’s artifact; my message failed because `lab post` needs an explicit message option. I’ll read the artifact and its evidence to extract the code blob, split, and model details before designing an independent test.

The artifact’s declared evidence run differs from the run cited in the board message, so I’ll inspect both rather than assume the headline numbers match. I’ll also fetch the submitted code to reproduce its exact pipeline.

The artifact’s declared evidence is the same run whose code blob it exposes, and the recorded CV supports its headline. I’ll inspect the code and output files to check exact splits, thresholds, and what can be compared fairly in a linked extension.

I’ll investigate the small steel-strength dataset independently, comparing regularized and tree-based models with composition-fraction features against the supplied baseline under the same five-fold protocol.

The accepted band-gap result is useful context but not a direct extension of my brief. I’ll focus on steel yield-strength prediction, compare composition-feature regressors against the supplied baseline on the same five-fold split, and only publish a model if validation supports it.

The fetched code is a single file rather than an extracted directory, so my attempted source inspection did not reach `run.py`. I’ll identify its format, then inspect and run it locally through `lab exec` as the reproduction baseline.
The steel experiment stopped on an invalid SVR gamma setting, so it produced no evidence. I’ll correct the parameter mapping and rerun the validation sweep.

I’ll test whether the fixed 0.5 cutoff is robust rather than tune it on the same folds used to report performance. I’ll use the founder’s code blob as an explicit input, compare prespecified thresholds on repeated held-out folds, and evaluate a cutoff selected on one split on independent splits.

ExtraTrees with one-leaf minimum and all composition features was strongest in the tuning run. I’ll now check it against the exact reference baseline across fresh repeated folds, and make the same compact model available for held-out prediction.

The steel set is small and compositionally structured, so I’ll compare the Magpie-lite baseline with direct elemental fractions and several regularized/tree models using identical shuffled five-fold splits. I’ll keep the validation procedure reproducible and make the eventual prediction script train on all available labels.

The founder’s code blob is a ZIP containing the model functions. I’ll reuse those exact feature and hurdle functions, then compare a small, preregistered set of probability thresholds over repeated shuffled five-fold splits; this isolates cutoff sensitivity without swapping in a different model.

The steel composition-identity ExtraTrees model substantially improves the same five-fold validation protocol over the reference. I’ll publish it with the executable prediction code, then check for collaborator work to replicate or materially extend.

I’ve located the founder’s exact code archive and will reuse its feature construction and hurdle components. First I’ll inspect the auxiliary module and gap distribution, then run a threshold sensitivity audit with fixed, repeated splits.

I’ve published validated findings for band gaps and steels. I’ll now test whether explicit elemental fractions also improve experimental metal/nonmetal classification, and will avoid making a claim unless the held-out prediction test has a plausible validation gain.

Direct elemental fractions with ExtraTrees substantially beat the Magpie-lite baseline on the prescribed folds. I’ll check whether that gain is stable across shuffled splits and whether removing all-zero elemental columns or transforming trace fractions improves it further before selecting the final model.

The chosen model beats the baseline across all 10 repeated five-fold splits, with lower MAE on every seed. I’ll save the self-contained held-out prediction script and publish a prediction-test contribution grounded in that recorded comparison.

I’ll evaluate threshold sensitivity on repeated outer folds and select thresholds only from nested out-of-fold predictions, so the reported selected-threshold performance is measured on data not used for selection. I’ll reuse the founder’s archived feature function directly and include calibration diagnostics.

The prediction script is stored as a blob and is self-contained apart from the public dataset and standard scientific Python libraries. I’ll publish the measured cross-validation comparison and specify the evaluator’s hidden-steel prediction test.

My first audit run failed because the founder-code input was not at the path or in the format I assumed; no metrics were produced. I’ll inspect the mounted input layout in a recorded run, then adjust the loader and rerun the audit.

The contribution passed its live evidence and code checks. I’ll check whether other researchers have steel results to compare against and confirm the artifact is visible to the community before doing further robustness checks.

The founder has an accepted steel finding on a similar feature approach, so I’ll inspect it and seek a meaningful extension rather than leave two redundant results. I’ll also share my validation result for coordination.

The founder’s model combines elemental fractions with Magpie descriptors, while mine uses fractions alone. I’ll inspect their released code and test whether adding those descriptors improves my simpler approach, explicitly treating that as an extension of their finding.

Steel interim: my normalized-element-fraction ExtraTrees (800 trees) scored 86.94 MPa mean pooled MAE across 10x5 shuffled CV, versus baseline 130.37 MPa; code blob d06bc0151c466e99c1c38726fa3f4a5ae8fad8361766795110b6c35a5c388db4, evidence exec-ecc4e04d. I found founder's related steels finding and will test Magpie-feature extension.

The recorded inspection shows the code blob is a tar archive mounted as one file, not an extracted directory. I’ll read `run.py` from that archive and rerun the audit; the previous failed attempt produced no metrics and won’t be used as evidence.
The founder’s released code arrived as an archive, so I’ll extract it and inspect its feature construction to set up a fair extension test using the same folds.

The founder’s released implementation uses elemental fractions, Magpie descriptors, and a two-leaf model, while my result used fractions alone. I’ll use their released feature code in a paired repeated-fold experiment to test whether adding Magpie features helps under identical splits and model settings.

The extension run failed because the baseline helper wasn’t on Python’s import path in the execution environment. I’ll load it from `$DATA_DIR/baselines` explicitly and rerun the paired comparison with the founder’s code input.

My previous edit didn’t move the import, so the same missing-module error recurred. I’ll correct the file ordering directly, using the execution environment’s `$DATA_DIR` path, and rerun the comparison.

The input blob is mounted as an archive file rather than an extracted directory. I’ll adapt the experiment to read the founder’s `run.py` from that archive, ensuring the comparison genuinely consumes the released code.

Element fractions plus aggregate descriptors modestly improve metal/nonmetal classification; I’ll make the best validation model the held-out default and rerun the script before publishing. I’ll continue seeking a substantive link to collaborators’ accepted work.

The audit’s Brier score used the positive-gap probabilities against the zero-gap labels, so that calibration diagnostic was reversed; I won’t rely on it. The outer-fold MAEs suggest a possible small gain at threshold 0.6, but nested threshold selection barely changed performance and chose different cutoffs across folds. I’ll rerun with the correct calibration target and paired fold comparisons before deciding what to publish.

The first fetched-metrics check used the wrong threshold-key format, so it did not establish a paired comparison. I’ll correct that with a fresh recorded audit: repeat the same folds for thresholds 0.5 and 0.6, fix the calibration-label direction, and measure whether the cutoff gain is consistent. I’ll make the same code produce paired predictions for a held-out comparison test if the CV evidence supports an extension.

The second run was unexpectedly routed into evaluation mode, where this execution had no hidden input files; again, it produced no metrics. I’ll make evaluation mode conditional on actual input availability and rerun the cross-validation audit.

The paired run suggests that adding Magpie descriptors did not help, but the founder’s evaluator path deploys a two-model fraction-only ensemble. To make the collaboration test direct and fair, I’ll compare my single-leaf ExtraTrees model against that exact deployed ensemble on identical repeated folds.

The explicit-element identity Random Forest improves metal-classification error by a potentially meaningful margin. I’ll publish it with its held-out prediction test, then check whether collaborators have results to reproduce or extend.

My metal-classification finding exposed a typo in the test’s code ID, so I’ll correct it using the recorded experiment and retain the uploaded script as its code artifact. A collaborator has also published a related steels result; I’ll inspect it for a genuine, measured extension.

I found a malformed code ID in the metal-classification test; I’ll republish a corrected version. A collaborator’s steel contribution is now accepted, so I’ll inspect and run their code as the basis for a direct extension rather than merely restating our overlapping result.
I’ll correct the metal-classification artifact’s test code reference, then examine how to execute the accepted collaborator steel model so any extension directly uses their published work.

The paired validation shows my single-leaf fraction model outperforming the founder’s deployed fraction-only ensemble on the same folds; adding Magpie descriptors also did not improve the tested model. I’ll package the direct model-versus-model held-out comparison so this result materially extends the founder’s work.

The collaborator’s accepted steel model uses elemental fractions alone. I’ll build a measurable extension that reuses their published implementation as the reference arm and tests whether adding Magpie descriptors improves its predictions, explicitly consuming their code blob in the experiment.

I’ll compare the collaborator’s accepted element-fraction model with a combined fraction-plus-Magpie extension using identical steel CV splits. The experiment will explicitly receive their published code blob, so a successful result can be a genuine extension.
I’ll check the input-blob interface before designing the extension, so the experiment can actually consume the collaborator’s published code and document a valid relationship.

I’ll test a direct extension of the collaborator’s accepted steel model: keep their published ExtraTrees configuration and normalized elemental fractions as one arm, and add Magpie descriptors as the other. I’ll load the accepted model’s parser, featurizer, and model definition from its supplied code blob, then compare both arms on identical folds.

The experiment failed because I assumed the accepted code would be mounted under `/in/accepted`; the guide specifies `$IN_DIR/NAME`. I’ll inspect the actual input mount and update the loader accordingly before rerunning.
The accepted code blob may be mounted as a single file rather than an unpacked directory, which my loader failed to account for. I’ll make it accept either form and rerun the same comparison.

In the corrected five-repeat audit, cutoff 0.6 had lower MAE than 0.5 in 16 of 25 paired folds, with a mean gain of about 0.008 eV; it was not uniformly better. I’ll make the 0.6 model’s held-out output directly comparable to the supplied baseline, rerun the evidence with the final test code, and publish this as a linked extension with that limitation explicit.

The accepted steel-model extension ran successfully: adding Magpie descriptors worsened five-fold MAE. I’ll publish this as a measured extension of the collaborator’s result, using the accepted code blob as an experiment input and providing paired held-out predictions for evaluation.

I tested a direct extension of findin-5133e252: your accepted fraction-only ExtraTrees vs same model plus Magpie descriptors, using your code blob. On paired five-folds it was 89.72 vs 91.72 MPa; published extension findin-<new id> as soon as returned. Magpie augmentation appears unhelpful here.

The repeated-split test supports the steel improvement, with untransformed elemental fractions and small-leaf ExtraTrees leading. I’ll test a few additional tree settings and inspect how to build on the accepted hurdle-model result without overstating the relationship.

The steel extension was accepted with valid evidence and a consumed collaborator code input. I’ll check the auditor and other researchers’ progress, then prioritize any opportunity to test a substantive improvement or refine an existing finding.

The direct paired run shows a modest but consistent validation advantage for single-leaf ExtraTrees over the founder’s deployed two-model ensemble. I’ll publish it as an extension, with a held-out comparison that tests both scripts on the same hidden alloys.

Follow-up steel result: direct paired 10x5 CV comparison of a 600-tree leaf-1 fraction ExtraTrees model vs the leaf-2/3 ensemble deployed by findin-8f91977f gives 87.02 vs 89.92 MPa MAE (exec-8e98eccb). The run consumed the founder's released code blob. I am publishing a held-out paired comparison as an extension.

The steel gain persists across repeated folds and is large enough to justify a held-out prediction test. Before publishing, I’ll check the required contribution fields and retrieve the accepted hurdle model’s implementation to assess whether its classification stage can be extended to experimental metal labels.

I’ll tune composition-derived glass-forming classifiers against the reference using the same five-fold split, focusing on tree depth, minimum leaf size, class weighting, and composition-distribution features. In parallel, I’ll recruit independent checks of the band-gap result and candidate model improvements for glass formation.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow, then locate the founder’s accepted gap and steel results so I can reproduce or stress-test them on held-out splits.

I’ll first build a clean steel prediction script that reproduces the comparison on the baseline’s five-fold protocol and emits evaluator-format predictions. I’ll also inspect whether the accepted hurdle model’s code can support a genuine extension to the separate metal-classification dataset.

I’ll first check the experiment and publishing requirements, inspect the glass data and baselines, and review the founder’s existing work so my experiments can extend or test it rather than duplicate it.
I’ll find the founder’s published findings and inspect the baseline/data formats, then choose a held-out robustness test that directly reproduces or challenges their claims.
I’ll inspect the glass dataset, baseline implementation, recorded experiments, and community artifacts to identify a useful extension and the correct prediction-test format.
I’ll inspect the accepted hurdle and steel claims plus their experiment records and code blobs, so the next tests can be faithful paired reproductions rather than unrelated models.

The accepted band-gap model’s hurdle stage classifies whether a compound has a positive gap—the same metal/nonmetal distinction used by `expt_is_metal`. I’ll inspect its feature and classifier implementation, then test that transfer directly against the metal-label baseline while explicitly consuming the accepted code as an input.

The glass dataset contains formula strings and likely repeated alloy families, so I’ll inspect its label balance and composition-family structure, then check whether the founder has already established a glass result before choosing a complementary CV design.

The steel findings already include a published fraction-only model, and the accepted gap finding publishes its hurdle code. I’ll retrieve both scripts and their full test specifications, then run paired robustness checks using those exact implementations as required.

The metal dataset is balanced, making a direct classification comparison appropriate. I’ll extract the accepted model’s classifier settings and feature construction so the extension can test whether its hurdle classifier transfers beyond band-gap regression.

The formula strings are unique, but many examples share the same element system, making random-fold validation potentially optimistic. I’ll inspect the founder’s two glass runs and their published work, then compare random and system-grouped validation before deciding which improvement is credible.

I’ve retrieved the accepted hurdle and steel fraction-model code. I’ll inspect their scripts and dataset schemas to identify a meaningful robustness test, especially whether the gains persist across repeated splits rather than only the original shuffled folds.

The fetched blob paths are files rather than unpacked directories, so I’ll inspect their contents and the recorded runs before setting up paired robustness experiments that explicitly consume the accepted code blobs.

The accepted code blobs appear to be packaged files rather than directories. I’ll identify their archive format and inspect the relevant recorded metrics, then run the accepted model code directly with its blob supplied as an experiment input.

The current model already beats the reference, and the collaboration comparison is published. I’ll test whether biasing ExtraTrees toward dilute alloying-element concentrations or transforming the target improves on the single-leaf model, using identical repeated folds.

The gap hurdle’s original five-fold result is reproducible from its recorded run, and steel has independent repeated-CV evidence. I’ll now inspect the published scripts and build paired repeated-split tests that directly reuse the accepted implementations, focusing on whether the hurdle and steel advantage remain robust to split choice.

I’ll use paired repeated five-fold splits to test whether the accepted gap hurdle’s gain over the baseline survives beyond the single reported split, and compare the accepted steel fraction model against the founder’s later ensemble on identical folds. Both accepted code blobs will be passed as experiment inputs and used directly.

The accepted model’s ExtraTrees hurdle classifier and composition features provide a concrete method to test on metal labels. First I’ll lock down the steel result with the best stable fraction-only ExtraTrees model and evaluator-compatible prediction output.

I’ll design a paired repeated-CV extension that executes the accepted gap script and steel fraction code supplied as `lab exec` inputs, then adds unseen-input predictions for evaluator testing. First I’m checking the scripts’ prediction interfaces so the extension preserves the published models faithfully.

The founder’s recorded glass result establishes a useful baseline (five-fold error 0.1168), while explicit element identity performed worse. I’ll test stoichiometric fraction and descriptor-based tree models against that same shuffled five-fold split, then assess promising candidates across additional seeds and element-system holdouts.

The first steel prediction run revealed that `EVAL_DIR` can be set even when held-out files are absent, so the script needs to distinguish an actual prediction input from a validation run. I’ll fix that before collecting clean evidence.

The accepted hurdle’s evaluator path is clear: it emits predictions from the published classifier-plus-regressor, while its original validation covered just one five-fold seed. I’ll extend that model to repeated paired folds; for steel, I’ll retrieve the founder’s accepted implementation so the robustness test uses the founder’s code, not a substitute.

The steel predictor now produces clean baseline-comparable evidence. I’ll test a direct extension of the accepted hurdle model’s feature construction and ExtraTrees classifier on experimental metal labels, passing the accepted code blob as an explicit input so the relationship is reproducible.

I’ll inspect the founder’s steel code and retrieve the accepted models through the experiment’s input mechanism. The planned comparison uses paired repeated folds, which can show whether the reported advantages are stable across split seeds.

I’ll test the accepted gap hurdle across 10 paired shuffled five-fold repeats against the supplied baseline, and make the same script emit both models’ predictions for the evaluator’s held-out comparison. It will load the published hurdle implementation from its supplied code blob.

The five-repeat result supports the hurdle model against the baseline, while the 0.6-versus-0.5 cutoff gain is modest and not universal. I’ll make the evaluator’s held-out comparison baseline versus the founder’s same hurdle model at 0.6, then publish the threshold audit as a linked extension without claiming 0.6 always wins.

The experiment environment sets `EVAL_DIR` even during validation, so my first harness incorrectly entered the held-out path and failed before producing evidence. I’ll make the gate require a nonempty evaluation directory, rerun the repeated-fold experiment, and preserve the published hurdle code as an input.

The Random Forest variant beat the baseline across three fold seeds, with validation error around 8.2% versus 9.3%. I’ll test weighted-variance descriptors and probability ensembles, then choose a fixed model and validate it with a clean evaluator-compatible script.

I’ll check whether a simple nearest-neighbor method or an ensemble can improve on the ExtraTrees predictor. I’ll evaluate each component over repeated folds and report its own pooled MAE, so any promising combination can be verified without relying on the previously tuned result alone.

Reusing the accepted model’s composition features and ExtraTrees classifier also improves metal-label cross-validation error over the baseline. I’ll compare a few classifier settings on the identical folds before choosing the extension’s held-out predictor.
A generated newline was escaped literally in the tuning script, causing a syntax error before the experiment ran. I’ll correct the import and rerun the classifier comparison.
The first repair didn’t match the literal `\n` characters in the file, so the script still failed at parse time. I’ll replace that exact text and verify the import lines before rerunning.
The import is now syntactically valid. I’ll rerun the same-fold classifier comparison and use its results to select the metal-task extension model.

The broader model search found the single-leaf ExtraTrees predictor remained strongest among individual models, while an equal-weight leaf-1/leaf-2 ensemble had a slightly lower cross-validated MAE. I’ll inspect the full ensemble results and check for community feedback before deciding whether that small gain merits a further held-out test.

My published model beats the reference baseline, and the paired follow-up extends the founder’s result. I’ll test whether averaging ExtraTrees models across feature-sampling settings or random seeds yields a reproducible further gain before deciding whether a new predictor is warranted.

The repeated-fold audit finds a small, directionally favorable cutoff shift, but it is not a guaranteed win on every split. I’ll make the evaluator directly compare the founder’s 0.5 cutoff against the 0.6 variant on hidden inputs; that tests the incremental extension rather than merely rechecking the hurdle model against the baseline.

The metal-task sweep found an ExtraTrees classifier using the accepted feature representation that improves the baseline error. I’ll verify the selected configuration over multiple shuffled five-fold splits, then use that same configuration for the held-out test.
The full parameter sweep exceeded the execution limit, so I’ll inspect recorded runs and narrow the search to a smaller, reproducible set of ExtraTrees settings.

The initial results favor ExtraTrees, but one split per design is not enough to establish robustness. I’ll compare a few fixed ExtraTrees and zero-aware variants on repeated random and reduced-formula-grouped folds against the exact reference baseline.

The corrected repeated-CV audit is complete and the final runner can emit paired predictions for the founder’s 0.5 cutoff and the audited 0.6 cutoff. I’ll check the comparison-test schema, package the runner, and publish a linked extension that reports the modest, nonuniform CV cutoff gain and leaves the hidden comparison as the decisive test.

The final runner is stored, and it consumes the founder’s code blob in both the experiment and evaluator test. I’ll publish the threshold extension with the repeated-CV result as evidence and a held-out paired comparison of 0.5 versus 0.6 as the decisive test.

The published cutoff comparison is now linked to the founder’s artifact. To stress-test whether that modest gain depends on random composition splitting, I’ll run a separate grouped-fold audit that keeps normalized formula families together and compares both cutoffs with the baseline.
